query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing nanoscale chemical short-range order (SRO) via a single, controlled anneal in a refractory BCC high-entropy alloy used as an intermediate layer will increase its through-thickness thermal conductivity at reactor-relevant temperatures without degrading high-temperature strength, compared to the same alloy in a maximally disordered solid-solution state.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline refractory BCC high-entropy alloy intermediate-layer material (e.g., Ta–W–Mo–V–Cr family), arc-melted and homogenized to a random solid solution with fine equiaxed grains (~10–50 µm), minimal pre-existing ordering or precipitates.
generation.intervention: Isothermal anneal at 0.45–0.60 of the alloy’s absolute melting temperature (Tm) for 12–48 hours in high-purity inert atmosphere (Ar) to induce chemical SRO while avoiding long-range ordering and significant grain growth.
generation.conditions: Evaluation under steady and cyclic thermal loading representative of plasma-facing components: 600–900°C bulk temperature, through-thickness heat flux causing a thermal gradient of ~5–20 W/mm, low-to-moderate mechanical bias (compressive/tensile) of 50–150 MPa, and no intentional irradiation during initial verification. Applicability expected up to doses where irradiation disordering dominates (to be bounded).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoscale SRO clusters (e.g., B2-like local pair correlations) within the BCC matrix that reduce chemical-disorder scattering of conduction electrons and phonons without creating a continuous brittle ordered phase; grain size and texture largely retained.
generation.mechanism: SRO reduces the configurational disorder that scatters charge carriers and phonons, increasing the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity (and total thermal conductivity) at high temperature. Concurrently, SRO increases lattice friction and can stabilize dislocation structures, preserving or slightly increasing high-temperature yield strength and fatigue resistance by impeding boundary sliding and dislocation motion without introducing brittle long-range order.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the same alloy kept maximally disordered, the SRO-annealed state will show a measurable increase in thermal conductivity at 600–900°C (expected improvement on the order of tens of percent; a conservative estimate is ~15–30% increase), while high-temperature yield strength and low-cycle fatigue life remain within ±10% of baseline or improve modestly. Electrical conductivity should increase in tandem, consistent with a Wiedemann–Franz relation, supporting an electronic-transport mechanism.
generation.baseline: Current intermediate-layer HEA implementations in the as-cast/as-homogenized, random solid-solution state with fine equiaxed grains and minimal chemical ordering.
generation.boundary: Benefits diminish or reverse if the anneal drives long-range ordering or significant second-phase precipitation that embrittles the alloy, if grain growth reduces mechanical integrity, or if irradiation doses or operating temperatures (>~0.7 Tm) disorder or destabilize SRO. Compositions lacking propensity for SRO will not exhibit the predicted improvement.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of thermal-conductivity increase is composition-dependent and may be smaller if SRO remains weak at the chosen anneal; mechanical effects could be neutral or slightly negative if grain growth occurs. No direct prior evidence is provided here; the mechanism and ranges are hypothesized based on general transport-scattering considerations in disordered alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare coupons from one refractory BCC HEA batch. Split into two groups: (A) solutionized to maximize disorder (e.g., high-temperature quench) and (B) annealed at 0.45–0.60 Tm for 12–48 h to induce SRO. Confirm SRO presence via diffuse scattering and/or atom-probe pair correlation analysis. Measure thermal and electrical conductivity versus temperature, and high-temperature mechanical properties. Compare under identical thermal-gradient and loading conditions.
measurements: Thermal diffusivity and specific heat (laser flash analysis) to compute thermal conductivity from 600–900°C
Electrical conductivity vs temperature to assess Wiedemann–Franz correlation
Synchrotron X-ray or neutron diffuse scattering to quantify SRO (Huang scattering/intensity changes)
Atom probe tomography or TEM diffraction to identify local chemical order/clustering
High-temperature tensile yield strength and modulus (e.g., at 700, 800, 900°C)
Low-cycle fatigue life under thermal cycling with superimposed mechanical bias
Grain size and texture (EBSD) to verify minimal grain growth and similar microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if group B does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity (>10% across 600–900°C) relative to group A while maintaining high-temperature yield strength within ±10% of group A, or if SRO cannot be detected in group B. A decrease in conductivity or a >10–15% degradation in strength or fatigue life under identical conditions also falsifies the hypothesis.
